Next we create a function load_reviews(), which will use gzip to unzip the downloaded Goodreads review JSON files and json to load the JSON files once they’re unzipped.

def load_reviews(file_name,
                 head=None):

    reviews = []
    count = 0

    with gzip.open(file_name) as file:
        for line in file:

            d = json.loads(line)
            count += 1

            _book_id = d['book_id']

            reviews.append(d['review_text'])

            # Break if we reach the Nth line
            if (head is not None) and (count > head):
                break

    return reviews

Now we apply the load_reviews() function. For each genre, we load and unzip the corresponding .json.gz file, e.g., poetry.json.gz, then we randomly sample 2000 Goodreads reviews and make a dictionary genre_reviews_dict of all these reviews.

genres = ['poetry', 'children', 'comics_graphic', 'fantasy_paranormal', 'history_biography', 'mystery_thriller_crime', 'romance', 'young_adult']
genre_reviews_dict = {}

for _genre in genres:
  print('Loading ' + _genre + '.json.gz')
  _reviews = load_reviews(_genre + '.json.gz')
  genre_reviews_dict[_genre] = random.sample(_reviews, 2000)

Split the data into training and test sets
When training a machine learning model, it is necessary to split your training data into two parts: a training set and a test set.
We will train our BERT model on the “training” set of Goodreads reviews and then we will evaluate how well it is performing by running it on the “test” set of Goodreads reviews that the model has never seen before.
Normally, to tune the hyperparameters, you should also create a “validation” set for tuning, and only use the “test” set once, at the end of all tuning. For simplicity, in this tutorial, we will only using a training and test set.

These are the arguments we’ll set in the HuggingFace TrainingArguments objects, which we’ll then pass to the HuggingFace Trainer object. There are many more possible arguments, but here we highlight the basics and some common gotchas.

title: Fine-tuning BERT for classification
text:
Fine-tune the BERT model
First, we define a custom evaluation function that returns the accuracy. You could modify this function to return precision, recall, F1, and/or other metrics.

def compute_metrics(pred):
  labels = pred.label_ids
  preds = pred.predictions.argmax(-1)
  acc = accuracy_score(labels, preds)
  return {
      'accuracy': acc,
  }

Then we create a HuggingFace Trainer object using the TrainingArguments object that we created above. We also send our compute_metrics function to the Trainer object, along with our test and train datasets.
Note: This is what we’ve been aiming for this whole time! All the work of tokenizing, creating datasets, and setting the training arguments was for this cell.

trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,                         # the instantiated 🤗 Transformers model to be trained
    args=training_args,                  # training arguments, defined above
    train_dataset=train_dataset,         # training dataset
    eval_dataset=test_dataset,           # evaluation dataset (usually a validation set; here we just send our test set)
    compute_metrics=compute_metrics      # our custom evaluation function
)

Time to finally fine-tune!
Be patient; if you’ve set everything in Colab to use GPUs, then it should take around 15 minutes to run, but if you’re running on CPU, it can take hours.
After every 10 steps (as we specified in the TrainingArguments object), the trainer will output the current state of the model, including the training loss, validation (“test”) loss, and accuracy (from our compute_metrics function).
You should see the loss going down and the accuracy going up. If instead they are staying the same or oscillating, you probably need to change the fine-tuning parameters.

title: Visual feature extraction
text:
Open in Colab Download notebook (.ipynb)
COMS 930 – Computational Methods
This notebook demonstrates how computers extract visual features from images. We will:
!pip -q install opencv-python matplotlib scikit-learn
import cv2
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from urllib.request import urlopen, Request
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

title: Visual feature extraction
text:
Load an Example Image

url = 'https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3f/Fronalpstock_big.jpg'
req = Request(url, headers={'User-Agent': 'Mozilla/5.0'})
img_array = np.asarray(bytearray(urlopen(req).read()), dtype=np.uint8)
img = cv2.imdecode(img_array, cv2.IMREAD_COLOR)
img = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)

plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))
plt.imshow(img)
plt.axis('off')
plt.title('Original Image')
plt.show()

title: Visual feature extraction
text:
Detect Visual Keypoints (Feature Extraction)
Keypoints are visually informative locations such as corners, edges, and texture changes.

gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY)

orb = cv2.ORB_create(nfeatures=500)
keypoints, descriptors = orb.detectAndCompute(gray, None)

img_keypoints = cv2.drawKeypoints(img, keypoints, None, color=(0,255,0), flags=0)

plt.figure(figsize=(10,7))
plt.imshow(img_keypoints)
plt.axis('off')
plt.title('Detected Visual Keypoints')
plt.show()

title: Visual feature extraction
text:
Inspect the Feature Vectors
For each keypoint, ORB computes a descriptor. This is a numerical summary of the local visual pattern around that keypoint.

Rows = keypoints
Columns = descriptor values

In other words, each row is a feature vector.

print('Number of keypoints:', len(keypoints))
print('Descriptor matrix shape:', descriptors.shape)
print('\nFirst feature vector:')
print(descriptors[0])

Number of keypoints: 500
Descriptor matrix shape: (500, 32)

First feature vector:
[212  49 187  96 248 108 113  80 186 141 231  24  22 151  65  58 176  60
  76  56  50 211 176   2 219 161  32 108 128  33  38  99]

title: Visual feature extraction
text:
What Does This Mean?
If the output shape is, for example, (500, 32), that means:

the algorithm found 500 keypoints
each keypoint is represented by a 32-number feature vector

These numbers summarize local edge and texture structure near the keypoint.

title: Visual feature extraction
section: Cluster the Feature Vectors into “Visual Words”
text:
Cluster the Feature Vectors into “Visual Words”
A Bag-of-Visual-Words approach groups similar feature vectors together.
Each cluster can be treated as a visual word.

k = 8  # number of visual words for a simple demo
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42, n_init=10)
cluster_labels = kmeans.fit_predict(descriptors)

print('Cluster counts (visual word frequencies):')
for i in range(k):
    print(f'Visual word {i}: {(cluster_labels == i).sum()} keypoints')

Cluster counts (visual word frequencies):
Visual word 0: 58 keypoints
Visual word 1: 71 keypoints
Visual word 2: 52 keypoints
Visual word 3: 78 keypoints
Visual word 4: 88 keypoints
Visual word 5: 50 keypoints
Visual word 6: 49 keypoints
Visual word 7: 54 keypoints

title: Visual feature extraction
text:
Visualize the Clusters in 2D
Each point below is one feature vector (one keypoint descriptor). PCA compresses the 32-dimensional descriptors into 2 dimensions so we can plot them.
Different colors = different clusters = different visual words.

pca = PCA(n_components=2)
desc_2d = pca.fit_transform(descriptors)

plt.figure(figsize=(8,6))
plt.scatter(desc_2d[:,0], desc_2d[:,1], c=cluster_labels, s=18)
plt.title('Feature Vectors Clustered into Visual Words')
plt.xlabel('PCA 1')
plt.ylabel('PCA 2')
plt.show()

title: Visual feature extraction
section: Connect This Back to the Theory
text:
Connect This Back to the Theory
The pipeline is:
image → keypoints → feature vectors → clusters → visual words
In a full Bag-of-Visual-Words analysis, we would repeat this across many images and then count how often each visual word appears in each image.

This should read in an object called igraph_data_list into your session of R. You can check that it worked with an ls() command. Once you have the data read in, you will be able to access the actual networks. They are stored in an R data type called a list. A list is R’s way of collecting a set of R objects that may have different types. You can access elements of a list using double square brackets with the number of the corresponding element of the list that you want to access. Each element of the list contains three things: the network, any node-level data (i.e., individual-level variables), and metadata about the network.
For this homework, I will ask you to work with diplomacy data, which is number 18 in the list. This network has a node level data file that gives information about the nodes. You can access that in the following code:
my_net <- igraph_data_list[[18]]$network
my_net_node_data <- igraph_data_list[[18]]$node_level_data
V(my_net)$name <- my_net_node_data$COUNTRY
## This graph was created by an old(er) igraph version.
## ℹ Call `igraph::upgrade_graph()` on it to use with the current igraph version.
## For now we convert it on the fly...
In the above, the first line turns the network in the 18th position in the list into an object named my_net. The second line creates a separate object called my_net_node_data that has the node-level data associated with the network that is 18th in the list. Finally, the third line changes the names of the vertices in the my_net network object to be the values in the my_net_node_data$COUNTRY column from the node-level data. There are other node-level attributes that you could add to the network with similar code if you so wished. By changing the name of the nodes to be the actual country names some of the parts of the assignment should be a little easier, but it is not actually necessary to do this.

def extract_emotion_info(thumbnail_url):
    try:
        # Analyze emotions in the image
        results = DeepFace.analyze(img_path=str(thumbnail_url), actions=['emotion'])

        # DeepFace sometimes returns a single dict or a list — handle both
        if isinstance(results, dict):
            results = [results]

        # Extract info for each face detected
        emotions_data = []
        for face_result in results:
            dominant = face_result['dominant_emotion']
            proportions = face_result['emotion']  # dictionary of all emotion scores
            emotions_data.append({
                'dominant_emotion': dominant,
                'emotion_proportions': proportions
            })

        return emotions_data

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Error analyzing thumbnail: {e}")
        return []
